title: Control Before Submission
shortDefinition: Submissions become reliable only when the opponent is held where the main escape structure is denied.
whyItMatters: Attacking too early loses mount, back, side control, or creates dangerous scrambles.
deepExplanation: Control before submission means isolating shoulder, neck, or hip line, blocking the first escape, then adding finishing pressure. It protects both effectiveness and safety.
beginnerView: Do not squeeze while the opponent can still rotate freely.
advancedView: Create a dilemma: they must choose between staying controlled or exposing the finish.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Control Before Submission during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Control Before Submission to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Control Before Submission is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Control Before Submission before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
